title: Métis and Non-Status Claims
intro: Who counts as Indian, paper promises, and the settlements that made self-government real.

terms.def: The Alberta land base protected since the 1938 Betterment Act across twelve settlements, with a dedicated trust fund from 1943.
The inquiry whose recommendations led Alberta to set aside Métis colonies with relief, medical care, and schooling.
Aboriginal people outside the Indian Act register, whose rights and claims run through different legal channels.

body: Start with who counts. The 1876 Indian Act defined an Indian as essentially a male person of Indian blood plus his wife and children, and everyone else fell off the lists. Scrip, involuntary enfranchisement, sexist marriage rules, and 1951 register errors multiplied the excluded, Dene leader Stephen Kakfwi, son of two Dené Tha' parents, counts federally as non-status because his grandfather once gave up status to open a business. Status and treaty rights then split apart: Bill C-31 restorations do not guarantee band membership, and Connie Chappell speaks for thousands asking whether Ottawa can tell her daughters they are not Native.

Legislation is not identity, the chapter insists, quoting a Windspeaker editorial that calls non-status Indian one of Canadian bureaucracy's most ridiculous inventions. The 1979 Native Council of Canada declaration answers with rights language: self-determination, guaranteed representation, an inalienable right to land and resources, and schooling in their own languages and customs, from a people who call themselves squatters on their own land.

Métis land rights begin in unkept paper. The Manitoba Act and Dominion Lands Act promised a Métis land base that mostly never arrived; most scrip-takers never received their land, communities scattered, and Ottawa would deal only with individuals, which invited fraud and speculation. Alberta hit crisis first, and organizers answered: Adrian Hope rode boxcars with eighty cents, sleeping under Edmonton's High Level Bridge, and in 1932 Joseph Dion, Malcolm Norris, Felix Calihoo, Peter Tomkins, and James Brady founded the Métis Association of Alberta, aiming at the province rather than Ottawa and demanding schools, doctors, and hunting and fishing rights too.

The province blinked. The 1934 Ewing Commission recommended farming colonies, and the 1938 Métis Population Betterment Act defined a Métis person, set aside twelve settlements chosen by a joint committee, and in 1943 created the trust fund for settlement resource income, though roughly $30 million in oil and gas wealth never reached it by the 1970s. The finish came in two strokes: the July 1989 Métis Settlements Accord gave eight settlements land ownership, self-government, and resource-revenue sharing, and the 1990 Métis Settlements Act wrote it into Alberta's constitution with elected five-person councils, the Métis Settlements General Council holding title, and an appeals tribunal. They remain Canada's only legislated Métis governments and the only Métis communities holding title, which is the chapter's closing question in miniature: what does a secure land base make possible?

example.title: See it in the theme
example.text: Pair this lesson with the Theme 1 scrip lesson: paper instead of treaty, then settlements instead of reserves. Then answer the reflection question in one sentence: the land base made legislation, taxation, and courts possible, which is self-government.

check.prompt: Why did the Métis Association of Alberta target the province instead of Ottawa in 1932?
check.sample: Sample response: federal petitions had failed for decades, while the province controlled Crown land, schools, medical care, and hunting and fishing permits, so pressure there won the Ewing Commission and then the 1938 Betterment Act.

title: A New Era and the First Modern Treaty
intro: Powley, the stages of settlement, James Bay, and the Dene-Métis claim.

terms.def: The 2003 Supreme Court ruling affirming constitutionally protected Métis harvesting rights and a duty to accommodate them.

terms.term: James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement
terms.def: The 1975 first modern treaty, trading Cree and Inuit title for land, cash, services, and a governing voice.
The formal approval that turns a negotiated final agreement into binding commitment, followed by signatures, legislation, and an implementation plan.

body: A new era opened in court. After decades caught between federal and provincial jurisdiction, and the first official point of contact arriving only with the 1985 Federal Interlocutor, Métis people won the 2003 Powley decision: the Supreme Court affirmed existing, constitutionally protected Métis rights, including harvesting rights, with a duty on all governments to accommodate them. Ottawa answered with about $10 million in 2004 to help Métis organizations build Powley-ready membership lists.

Settlements themselves run in stages worth memorizing. A Memorandum of Understanding commits everyone to talk, a Framework Agreement sets issues, process, and deadlines, then comes the Agreement-in-Principle, the longest stage, holding every deal that will shape the settlement. The Final Agreement details resources, money, self-government, and land ownership, and must be ratified by the Aboriginal group, the province or territory, and Canada before Parliament legislates it into force, with constitutional protection covering the deal and any self-government inside it.

James Bay wrote the template. When Premier Bourassa announced his massive hydro project on April 30, 1970, Cree and Inuit peoples who had never surrendered title organized under 22-year-old Chief Billy Diamond, Grand Chief Ted Moses, and Charlie Watt; a 1973 injunction briefly stopped construction, talks began, and the 1975 James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement, Canada's first modern treaty, traded title for $134 million to the Cree, over $91 million to the Inuit, school boards, health services, environmental committees, and 1.1 million square kilometres sorted into Category I, II, and III lands. The 1978 Northeastern Quebec Agreement added $9 million and school control for the Naskapi, the 1984 Cree-Naskapi Act became Canada's first Aboriginal self-government legislation, and Diamond and Watt went on to help draft Section 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982.

Northwest of there, the Dene and Métis of the Treaty Eleven region filed jointly in 1974, bound by descent and threatened alike by a proposed Mackenzie Valley pipeline across lands that Treaties Eight and Eleven had never properly reserved. Sixteen years later they initialled an Agreement-in-Principle, then judged it too thin on rights, asked to renegotiate, were refused, and split so each community could pursue its own course. The lesson travels: stages are only as good as the rights they protect.

example.title: Sort a settlement
example.text: Take James Bay through the stages: trigger (the 1970 dam announcement), pressure (the 1973 injunction), deal (the 1975 agreement and its land categories), and afterlife (the 1984 self-government act and Section 35). Every settled claim in the next two lessons fits the same skeleton.

check.prompt: Why does the chapter call James Bay the first modern treaty rather than just another treaty?
check.sample: Sample response: beyond land and cash it gave the Cree and Inuit governing roles, services, environmental voice, and land categories, then grew into the first self-government legislation and helped entrench Aboriginal rights in Section 35.
